ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Cardiology Referral — Susan B. Anthony

code.originalText: Primary care visit for breathlessness on exertion and ankle swelling

text.paragraph: New heart failure in an active 85-year-old woman, likely with preserved ejection fraction. Please confirm the diagnosis, review the echocardiogram, and advise on any specific cause and on therapy. [S]
Urgency: Routine, within two weeks; echocardiogram booked for the same morning. [S]

list.item: Does the echocardiogram confirm heart failure with preserved ejection fraction?
Is there any sign of a specific cause, such as cardiac amyloidosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, or significant valve disease, that would change treatment?
Do you agree with adding spironolactone once potassium and kidney function are stable?
Is cardiac rehabilitation or any further testing worthwhile at her level of activity?

text.paragraph: Three months of breathlessness after one flight of stairs or a long station platform, with ankle swelling by evening and two-pillow orthopnea. NT-proBNP 1650 pg/mL; ECG shows sinus rhythm and left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage, without atrial fibrillation. Blood pressure 158/86 mmHg. Furosemide 20 mg and empagliflozin 10 mg were started today. Never smoker, no diabetes, kidney function near normal (eGFR 64) [S]

list.item: Breathlessness and ankle swelling after travel threaten her lecture schedule. [S]
Does not want to be kept in bed or slowed down by treatment. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Susan B. Anthony was born on February 15, 1820, in Adams, Massachusetts, the second child of Daniel and Lucy Read Anthony. [D]
Anthony voted in the 1872 presidential election, was arrested at her Rochester home, and was convicted at Canandaigua, New York; she refused to pay the $100 fine. [D]

Her father, Daniel Anthony, who had not had a day's illness in forty years, was suddenly stricken in November 1862 with what was called acute neuralgia of the stomach and died two weeks later, on November 25, 1862, at 69. [D]
Her 1898 biography describes a long-lived family: her mother died at eighty-six, her paternal grandfather lived past ninety-seven, and both maternal grandparents died in their eighty-fourth year. [D]
In January 1891, after weeks of what seemed a persistent la grippe, Anthony collapsed at the Garrison home in Brookline, Massachusetts; pneumonia threatened and she kept to her room for a week. [D]

On July 26, 1895, near the end of an address at Lakeside, Ohio, Anthony stopped abruptly and fainted; from July 30 she spent a month in bed with what was called nervous prostration, described as her first serious illness in seventy-five years. [D]

Her biographer described her daily habits in the late 1890s: a cold sponge bath each morning, simple food, tea and coffee in moderation, a rest after meals and an hour's rest each afternoon, and fresh air and exercise every day, walking from the station after a day on the train. [D]

list.item: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, NYHA class II to III at diagnosis; synthetic modern diagnosis linked to the documented 1906 heart failure: active, confirmed [S]
Hypertensive heart disease with heart failure: active, confirmed [S]

Treat congestion with furosemide and start empagliflozin for HFpEF; move to as-needed furosemide guided by daily weights once euvolemic. Guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure (2022); 2023 ACC Expert Consensus Decision Pathway on Management of Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction (2023) [S]

Add low-dose spironolactone for HFpEF with blood pressure above target once potassium and kidney function are stable. Guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure (2022); 2023 ACC Expert Consensus Decision Pathway on Management of Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction (2023) [S]

Check a basic metabolic panel and magnesium one to two weeks after starting or changing diuretic, SGLT2 inhibitor, or mineralocorticoid antagonist therapy, then every three to six months; KCCQ-12 every three to six months. Guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, heart failure monograph (2026) [S]

Pneumococcal and RSV vaccination and a yearly high-dose influenza vaccine to lower the risk of respiratory infection in heart failure. Guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, heart failure monograph (2026) [S]
